title: Health Assessment & Nursing Skills: Musculoskeletal Assessment, Mobility & Fall Risk
html:
A musculoskeletal assessment evaluates bones, joints, muscles, posture, movement, strength, and how the client performs meaningful activities. The goal is not simply to label range of motion as normal or abnormal. The RN identifies pain, asymmetry, functional loss, fall risk, neurovascular compromise, and change from baseline, then translates those findings into safe mobility and prevention plans.

Learning goals

  • Collect a focused history of pain, injury, mobility, falls, and daily function.
  • Inspect posture, joints, muscles, transfers, balance, and gait safely.
  • Distinguish active from passive range of motion and assess muscle strength consistently.
  • Perform and interpret a focused distal neurovascular assessment.
  • Recognize fracture, dislocation, acute limb ischemia, and compartment-pressure warning patterns.
  • Create an individualized fall-prevention plan and document functional outcomes.

Begin with safety and function

Review the reason for care, prescribed activity level, weight-bearing status, fall-risk plan, pain treatment, recent surgery or injury, mobility-aid use, and physical or occupational therapy recommendations. Observe how the client moves in bed, reaches for objects, sits, rises, transfers, and walks during usual activity. Do not ask a client to stand merely to complete a checklist before verifying that standing is safe.

Assess airway, breathing, circulation, neurologic status, pain, vital signs, and distal perfusion when injury or acute change is present. Obvious deformity, an open injury, inability to bear weight after trauma, a shortened or rotated limb, a newly cool or pulseless extremity, rapidly increasing swelling, or severe pain out of proportion requires immediate protection, focused neurovascular assessment, and escalation. Avoid unnecessary movement or range-of-motion testing of a suspected fracture or dislocation.

Severe pain plus neurovascular change is an emergency pattern
Escalating pain—especially pain with passive stretch—tense swelling, paresthesia, weakness, pallor, coolness, or a diminishing pulse after injury, surgery, casting, or tight dressings can signal limb-threatening pressure or perfusion compromise. Do not wait for every sign or for the pulse to disappear before acting.

Ask about movement in daily life

Use PQRSTU for pain and clarify location, onset, mechanism, quality, severity at rest and with movement, timing, swelling, stiffness, weakness, numbness, clicking or locking, and treatments tried. Ask about recent trauma, falls and near falls, osteoporosis or fracture history, joint or muscle conditions, surgery, prostheses, back problems, neurologic disease, dizziness, and exercise or occupational demands.

Ask what the client could do before the current problem and what is different now. Assess turning in bed, sitting, standing, transferring, walking distance, stairs, toileting, bathing, dressing, meal preparation, work, sleep, and community access. Determine whether pain, weakness, breathlessness, fatigue, fear of falling, cognition, vision, footwear, continence urgency, environment, or medication effects limit function.

Identify the client’s usual cane, walker, brace, prosthesis, wheelchair, or other equipment and who assists at home. Ask whether the device fits, is available, and is used consistently. A mobility device can improve safety only when it is appropriate, fitted, maintained, and used correctly.

Inspect posture, alignment, and symmetry

With consent and adequate exposure, inspect the spine, shoulders, hips, extremities, joints, and muscles for alignment, symmetry, size, atrophy, swelling, redness, bruising, deformity, contracture, foot drop, wounds, and device pressure. Compare corresponding sides while accounting for dominant-side differences, prior surgery, and documented baseline.

Observe spontaneous movement and willingness to use each limb. Note guarding and nonverbal pain. Age may influence strength, muscle mass, and flexibility, but a new asymmetry, functional decline, or painful limitation should not be dismissed as normal aging.

Palpate gently and assess joints

Palpate bones, muscles, and joints for temperature, tenderness, swelling, and crepitus when appropriate. Support the limb and avoid forcing movement. A hot, swollen, painful joint—especially with fever or systemic illness—requires prompt evaluation. Painful crepitus, new instability, or focal bony tenderness after trauma is also concerning.

Document exact location rather than “joint pain.” Identify whether swelling is localized or diffuse and whether skin color, sensation, and distal perfusion are altered. Do not massage a newly swollen, warm, tender calf or use a provocative maneuver to rule thrombosis in or out.

Assess active motion before passive motion

Active range of motion is movement performed by the client and reflects joint mobility, muscle strength, coordination, willingness, and pain. Ask the client to move major joints through the safe expected motions while comparing sides. Note the point at which pain, weakness, stiffness, or substitution occurs.

If active motion is limited and fracture, dislocation, acute neurovascular threat, or other contraindication is not suspected, passive range of motion may help distinguish weakness from joint restriction. Stabilize the joint and move slowly only to the point of resistance or discomfort. Never force the joint or repeatedly reproduce pain. Passive motion that is also limited suggests a different pattern from full passive motion with impaired active movement, but the RN does not establish a medical diagnosis from this difference alone.

Grade strength consistently

Assess corresponding muscle groups using equal positioning and resistance. A common 0-to-5 scale ranges from no visible contraction to full movement against gravity and full resistance, but the RN should use the organization’s definitions consistently. Document the side, muscle group or action, grade, pain, and factors such as fatigue, comprehension, precautions, or restricted weight bearing.

Hand grasps alone do not represent total upper-extremity strength. Compare shoulder, elbow, wrist, hip, knee, and ankle actions as indicated. Avoid resistance testing across a painful acute injury or prohibited postoperative movement. New focal weakness also requires neurologic assessment.

Check distal neurovascular status

Before and after casting, splinting, surgery, traction adjustment by authorized personnel, or significant injury, assess distal pain, color, temperature, capillary refill, pulse, movement, and sensation. Compare with the opposite limb and prior findings. Ask about numbness, tingling, burning, increasing pressure, or inability to move digits.

A palpable pulse does not rule out early compartment pressure. Worsening pain out of proportion, pain with passive stretch, tense swelling, or new sensory or motor change requires urgent escalation. If a pulse is difficult to palpate, verify the landmark and use Doppler according to training and policy. Document the assessment before and after an intervention so change is visible.

Progress mobility in safe stages

When appropriate, assess strength and bed mobility before advancing to sitting at the edge of the bed, standing, transferring, and walking. Allow time for position changes and assess dizziness, blood pressure symptoms, pain, respiratory tolerance, fatigue, balance, and command following. Use the prescribed assistance level, footwear, gait belt, and device according to policy.

Observe base of support, posture, step length, foot clearance, symmetry, pace, arm swing, turning, and need to steady against furniture. Do not perform a gait or balance test when the client cannot stand safely. Defer it, document the limitation, and obtain appropriate assistance or rehabilitation input.

Fall risk is a plan, not just a score

Use the approved fall-risk tool, but also assess recent fall or near fall, gait and transfer ability, lower-extremity strength, cognition, impulsivity, dizziness, vision, continence urgency, medications, orthostatic symptoms, footwear, unfamiliar environment, tubes and equipment, and willingness to call for help. Risk can change after surgery, sedation, new illness, medication, or a change in mobility.

Match prevention measures to the client’s specific risks: keep the bed low and locked; provide a clear path, adequate lighting, nonslip footwear, call system and personal items within reach; schedule toileting; use prescribed devices; communicate the assistance level; and involve the client and family. Universal precautions support everyone, while individualized measures address why this client may fall. Reassess after any fall, near fall, medication change, transfer, or clinical deterioration.

Consider the multisystem cost of immobility

Limited mobility can contribute to pressure injury, secretion retention, atelectasis, venous stasis, constipation, urinary problems, deconditioning, contracture, orthostatic intolerance, sleep disruption, and loss of independence. Assess skin, breathing, circulation, elimination, nutrition, pain, mood, and cognition alongside movement. Implement prescribed repositioning, range of motion, mobility, circulation, and rehabilitation plans and evaluate tolerance.

Respect delegation and collaboration boundaries

Assistive personnel may help with assigned mobility, range-of-motion activity, repositioning, and observation for a stable client when competency, policy, and the care plan permit. The RN assesses readiness, sets the assistance level, communicates precautions, validates unexpected findings, performs focused neurovascular assessment, and evaluates the response. New pain, weakness, dizziness, inability to bear weight, or device concern must return to the RN before continuing activity.

Physical and occupational therapists contribute specialized mobility, device, and functional evaluation. Collaboration does not remove RN responsibility for ongoing safety assessment and change recognition.

Document function and response

Record pain at rest and movement; injury mechanism and timing; posture and alignment; joint findings; active and passive motion; strength by action and side; distal neurovascular status; bed mobility, transfer, gait, distance and assistance; device used; weight-bearing restrictions; fall risks and interventions; tolerance; communication; and reassessment. Replace “up with help” with the actual level of assistance and equipment.

For example: “1000: Before ambulation, reports new right-calf pain 7/10. Right calf visibly larger, warm and tender compared with left; pedal pulses present, color and sensation intact. Ambulation held; limb not massaged. RN notified provider at 1003 and maintained client at rest pending evaluation.” This documents the observation and safety response without declaring a diagnosis.

Clinical example

A client with a new lower-leg cast reports increasing pain despite the prescribed intervention. The toes are warm with a palpable pulse, but passive toe stretch sharply increases pain and sensation is newly reduced. The RN recognizes that a present pulse does not eliminate a developing pressure threat, stops routine mobility, completes and documents the focused neurovascular comparison, and initiates urgent evaluation.
